newsitem.title: UK: TR European bid for KEPIT seen dying.
newsitem.headline: TR European bid for KEPIT seen dying.

text.p: A hostile bid from the TR European Growth Fund Plc for the Kleinwort European Investment Trust Plc (KEPIT) looks dead in the water after new proposals to restructure the ailing 500 million pound fund, investors say.

On Tuesday, the independent board offered investors in KEPIT the opportunity to exit the fund and claim cash, to continue investing in European privatisations, or to invest in a general European unit trust.
"I would be surprised if TR European gets the backing of 10 percent of the KEPIT shareholders," said a senior fund manager.
TR European is due to announce acceptances for its hostile bid for KEPIT on Friday, but investors believe the proposals from the board address all the options shareholders wanted.
"There is something for everyone. It gives people a choice in terms of a cash exit" said Colin Mclean of Scottish Value Management, whose Scottish Value Trust Plc has a four percent stake in KEPIT.
"Investors will be able to get out of the underlying stock at the offer price," said Mclean who said he would probably opt mostly for the cash option.

The board today recommended that investors choose between units in a new Kleinwort Benson European Privatisation Trust, units in an existing European unit trust, the M&G European and General Fund, or units in the Kleinwort Benson Money Market Trust, which can be held as an investment or redeemed for cash.

"The independent directors of KEPIT believe that it is important to provide shareholders with the opportunity to retain an investment in a fund dedicated to privatisation in Europe," said Shane Ross, chairman of the board.

He said the new Kleinwort privatisation unit trust would have a wider mandate than those for KEPIT, which foundered as European privatisations failed to deliver the spectacular gains British state firms showed when they were sold in the 1980s.

Proposals from M&G will allow a portion of KEPIT's assets to be transferred to M&G European without incurring dealing costs and Kleinwort Benson would waive two million pounds in management fees arising from any termination of its contract.
"Where net asset value is now, the deal being recommended is probably worth 98 pence per share," said Scottish Value's Mclean.

TR European made an improved cash bid of 96.2 pence per share for the investment trust on August 23, but is also offering investors the opportunity to subscribe for its top performing fund if they choose.

"TR European did everyone a favour by opening the debate, but it would have looked better for them, as well as costing less, if they had joined the list of proposals rather than continuing with a hostile bid," said Mclean.
Shareholders in KEPIT will vote on the board's proposals, but the board has continually opposed TR European's offer and believes its proposals offer better value than the hostile bid.
"The independent directors believe the recommended proposal is clearly superior to TR European's offers...We urge you not to accept TR European's offers," said Ross.
Whatever the future of KEPIT, Ross, an Irish member of parliament and journalist will lose his job.

Opinions on his performance are divided, one small investor called him an undertaker when he remarked that with the benefit of hindsight, 1994 might not have been the best time to launch a European privatisation investment vehicle.
"This offer shows that the board headed by Shane Ross has been best placed to look after the interests of shareholders," said Simon White, a director of KEPIT.
